subject: Copywriting
title: The Wall Street Journal Letter
description: Learn The Wall Street Journal Letter in one minute.

hook.text: One sales letter ran for 28 years and generated over $2 billion in revenue.

buildup.text: Martin Conroy wrote it for The Wall Street Journal in 1975.

discovery.text: The difference? One read the Journal, the other didn't. The story sold knowledge as the competitive edge.

twist.text: The letter had no gimmicks, no offers, no countdown timers. Pure storytelling. The narrative did all the selling.

climax.text: $2 billion from one letter, unchanged for 28 years. No A/B test could beat it. Perfect copy exists.

punchline.text: Two men, one letter, $2 billion. The greatest sales letter ever.

quiz.question: How long did the Wall Street Journal sales letter run?

details.summary: The Wall Street Journal's 'Two Young Men' letter is the most successful sales letter in history, generating over $2 billion in subscriptions across 28 years. Its genius was simple: two identical men, same education, same company — but one read the Journal and rose to the top.
details.whyItMatters: This letter demonstrates the timeless power of narrative contrast in sales copy. By showing two divergent outcomes from one small decision, it made subscribing feel like an investment in future success rather than an expense.
takeaways: The letter ran virtually unchanged for 28 years, proving timeless copy exists
Narrative contrast — two paths, one choice — is a supremely persuasive structure
The letter sold aspiration and identity, not a newspaper subscription

faq.question: Why did the Two Young Men letter work for so long?
faq.answer: It tapped into a universal human fear: falling behind peers. The narrative structure was personal, relatable, and emotionally compelling. It didn't sell information — it sold the possibility of becoming the successful man instead of the average one.

faq.question: What made this letter structure so effective?
faq.answer: The before/after contrast with identical starting points made the difference feel attributable to one factor: the Journal subscription. This eliminated counter-arguments ('he had advantages I don't') and made the purchase decision feel logical and inevitable.
